cards.back: To match or surpass something by imitation. Example: 'Developing nations often emulate the economic strategies of industrialised countries in hopes of achieving similar growth.'
To declare one's public approval or support of something. Example: 'The World Health Organisation endorsed the new guidelines for reducing sugar consumption in children.'
A person or thing that is mysterious or difficult to understand. Example: 'The sudden disappearance of the ancient civilisation remains an enigma that archaeologists have yet to solve.'
A perfect example of a particular quality or type. Example: 'The city's public transport system is often cited as the epitome of efficient urban planning.'
Fair and impartial. Example: 'An equitable distribution of resources is essential for reducing poverty in marginalised communities.'
To destroy completely; to put an end to. Example: 'Global vaccination campaigns have been instrumental in efforts to eradicate infectious diseases such as polio.'
Not even or regular in pattern or movement; unpredictable. Example: 'Erratic rainfall patterns have made it increasingly difficult for farmers to plan their planting seasons.'
To increase rapidly in intensity or magnitude. Example: 'Tensions between the two nations escalated following the dispute over territorial waters.'
To adopt or support a cause, belief, or way of life. Example: 'The organisation espouses the principles of sustainable development and corporate responsibility.'
To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse. Example: 'Poor urban planning can exacerbate the effects of flooding during the monsoon season.'
To serve as a typical example of something. Example: 'Finland's education system exemplifies how prioritising teacher quality can lead to exceptional student outcomes.'
To make an action or process happen sooner or be accomplished more quickly. Example: 'Digital record-keeping can expedite the processing of visa applications significantly.'
Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion or doubt. Example: 'The research paper provides explicit instructions for replicating the experimental methodology.'
Becoming more and more rapid; growing at an increasingly fast rate. Example: 'The exponential growth of social media usage has fundamentally altered how people consume news.'
To invent or concoct something, typically with deceitful intent. Example: 'The journalist was dismissed after it was discovered that she had fabricated key details in her report.'
One side or aspect of something. Example: 'The study examines multiple facets of childhood development, including emotional, social, and cognitive dimensions.'
A mistaken belief, especially one based on unsound reasoning. Example: 'The assumption that correlation implies causation is a common fallacy in statistical analysis.'
Possible and practical to accomplish. Example: 'Solar energy has become a more feasible alternative to fossil fuels as technology costs continue to decline.'
Having or displaying a passionate intensity. Example: 'The environmental activist made a fervent plea for immediate action on deforestation.'
To rise and fall irregularly in number or amount. Example: 'Oil prices tend to fluctuate in response to geopolitical events and changes in global demand.'
To prevent or obstruct something anticipated by taking action in advance. Example: 'Early intervention programmes aim to forestall the development of behavioural problems in at-risk youth.'
Inspiring fear or respect through being impressively large, powerful, or capable. Example: 'Climate change poses a formidable challenge that requires coordinated international cooperation.'
To encourage the development of something. Example: 'Inclusive classroom practices foster a sense of belonging among students from diverse backgrounds.'
Incapable of producing any useful result; pointless. Example: 'Without addressing the root causes of poverty, short-term aid programmes may prove futile.'
To shock or excite someone into taking action. Example: 'The alarming report on ocean pollution galvanized public support for stricter waste management policies.'
To gather or collect something, especially support or approval. Example: 'The proposal garnered widespread support from both academics and industry leaders.'
Relevant to a subject under consideration. Example: 'The candidate's work experience, while impressive, was not entirely germane to the position being offered.'
Fond of company; sociable. Example: 'Gregarious individuals tend to thrive in collaborative work environments and team-based projects.'
To hinder or impede the movement or progress of something. Example: 'Insufficient funding continues to hamper scientific research in many developing countries.'
A person or thing that announces or signals the approach of something. Example: 'The sharp decline in consumer spending was seen as a harbinger of the coming economic downturn.'
To control and make use of natural resources or energy. Example: 'Engineers are developing new methods to harness tidal energy as a sustainable power source.'
To create difficulties for someone or something, resulting in delay or obstruction. Example: 'Language barriers can significantly hinder the integration of refugee populations into host communities.'
Characterised by the treatment of the whole person, taking into account all factors. Example: 'A holistic approach to healthcare considers psychological well-being alongside physical symptoms.'
Based on or serving as a hypothesis; supposed but not necessarily true. Example: 'The researcher outlined a hypothetical scenario in which sea levels rise by two metres by 2100.'
To weaken or damage something, especially a faculty or function. Example: 'Chronic sleep deprivation can significantly impair an individual's ability to concentrate and make decisions.'
Treating all rivals or disputants equally; fair and just. Example: 'An impartial review panel was assembled to evaluate the competing grant applications.'
To delay or prevent someone or something by obstructing them. Example: 'Excessive regulation can impede innovation by discouraging entrepreneurs from launching new ventures.'
Of vital importance; crucial. Example: 'It is imperative that governments invest in education to prepare the workforce for the demands of a digital economy.'

The force or energy with which something moves, or something that makes a process happen more quickly. Example: 'The pandemic provided the impetus for many businesses to accelerate their adoption of remote working technologies.'
Implied though not plainly expressed. Example: 'There is an implicit assumption in the study that all participants had equal access to digital resources.'
Not resulting from or achieved through deliberate planning; unintentional. Example: 'The inadvertent release of confidential data highlighted serious flaws in the company's cybersecurity protocols.'
A thing that motivates or encourages someone to do something. Example: 'Tax incentives for electric vehicles have proven effective in encouraging consumers to adopt greener transport options.'
Originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native. Example: 'The preservation of indigenous languages is critical to maintaining cultural diversity worldwide.'
Absolutely necessary; essential. Example: 'Access to clean water is indispensable for the health and well-being of any community.'
Existing in something as a permanent, essential, or characteristic attribute. Example: 'There are inherent risks in any medical procedure, which must be communicated clearly to patients.'
Inborn; natural rather than learned. Example: 'The debate over whether language ability is innate or acquired remains a central issue in linguistics.'
Proceeding in a gradual, subtle way, but with very harmful effects. Example: 'The insidious effects of workplace stress often go unnoticed until they manifest as serious health conditions.'
Necessary to make a whole complete; fundamental. Example: 'Critical thinking skills are integral to success in higher education and professional life.'
Very complicated or detailed. Example: 'The intricate relationship between genetics and environment makes predicting disease outcomes extremely challenging.'
Belonging naturally; essential. Example: 'Intrinsic motivation, such as personal curiosity, is often more effective than external rewards in sustaining long-term learning.'
To overwhelm with things or people to be dealt with. Example: 'Hospitals were inundated with patients during the peak of the influenza outbreak.'
To cite or appeal to something as an authority or justification. Example: 'The defence attorney invoked the precedent set by a landmark Supreme Court ruling.'
Not able to be undone or altered. Example: 'Scientists warn that some of the damage caused by deforestation may be irreversible within our lifetime.'
Having, showing, or done with good judgement or sense. Example: 'Judicious use of antibiotics is essential to prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria.'
To place close together for contrasting effect. Example: 'The author juxtaposes urban affluence with rural deprivation to highlight the extent of regional inequality.'
Existing but not yet developed or manifest; hidden or concealed. Example: 'The programme was designed to unlock the latent potential of students from disadvantaged backgrounds.'
Deserving praise and commendation. Example: 'While the initiative's goals are laudable, its implementation has been hampered by a lack of adequate resources.'
To use something to maximum advantage. Example: 'Companies that leverage data analytics effectively can gain a significant competitive advantage in the market.'
Expressed clearly; easy to understand. Example: 'The textbook provides a lucid explanation of economic theory that is accessible to undergraduate students.'
To display or show a quality or feeling by one's acts or appearance. Example: 'Anxiety can manifest in various physical symptoms, including headaches and difficulty sleeping.'
An official order or commission to do something. Example: 'The government issued a mandate requiring all public buildings to meet new energy efficiency standards.'
Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise. Example: 'Meticulous record-keeping is essential in clinical trials to ensure the integrity of the data.'
To make something less severe, serious, or painful. Example: 'Planting trees in urban areas can help mitigate the effects of the heat island phenomenon.'
Of great importance or significance, especially in having a bearing on future events. Example: 'The discovery of penicillin was a momentous breakthrough in the history of modern medicine.'
Lacking interest or excitement; dull and ordinary. Example: 'Automation has the potential to free workers from mundane tasks, allowing them to focus on creative problem-solving.'
So small or unimportant as to be not worth considering. Example: 'The difference in test scores between the two groups was negligible and not statistically significant.'
To care for and encourage the growth or development of something. Example: 'Effective mentoring programmes nurture young talent by providing guidance and professional support.'
No longer produced or used; out of date. Example: 'Rapid technological advancement has rendered many traditional manufacturing processes obsolete.'

A seemingly absurd or contradictory statement or situation that may nonetheless be true. Example: 'The paradox of globalisation is that it simultaneously promotes cultural exchange and threatens cultural homogeneity.'
Spreading widely throughout an area or a group of people. Example: 'The pervasive influence of social media on political discourse has raised concerns about misinformation.'

Dealing with things sensibly and realistically based on practical considerations. Example: 'A pragmatic approach to urban planning balances environmental concerns with the economic needs of the community.'
To increase rapidly in number; to multiply. Example: 'Online learning platforms have proliferated in recent years, offering courses on virtually every subject.'
Able to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions. Example: 'Communities that invest in disaster preparedness tend to be more resilient in the face of natural catastrophes.'
To provide evidence to support or prove the truth of something. Example: 'The researchers were unable to substantiate their initial hypothesis with the data collected.'
Clear and definite; real and able to be shown or touched. Example: 'The new policy has already produced tangible improvements in air quality across the metropolitan area.'
